guest: Compilation (Greg Newman, Tom Dante, Aaron Brown, Mike Ingram, John Moulton, Raoul Pal, Larry Hite, Rob)
markets: oil futures, FX, bonds, ES futures, macro
edge_principles: Decide the invalidation price before entry and size so that the distance to it equals a fixed slice of capital (risk per trade = (entry - stop) / capital, Larry Hite style).
Place the stop where the thesis is wrong given normal volatility, not at an arbitrary tight distance that ordinary noise will hit.
Do not reflexively move stops to breakeven; a 'free trade' often gets scratched at support right before the intended move, and reward/risk changes as the trade progresses.
Edge = win rate x payoff; a high-win-rate style can live with ~1:1 targets, so do not distort stop/target to hit a fixed R ratio that ignores market structure.
Decide early in a trade whether it is a 'run it' trade (higher-timeframe move) or a level-to-level trade; manage accordingly.
Never average into a losing position.
Keep risk constant once a strategy is adopted instead of starting tiny and scaling up late, which leaves the largest exposure for when the edge decays.
Evaluate a model only on blocks of trades (about a month for a day trader), not after a few losses.
Risk limits should bind at survival-threatening levels; over-protection kills opportunity.
Know average win, average loss and trade frequency; changing frequency changes the risk model even with the same stop.
notes: Risk-management compilation; no concrete intraday setups, but useful sizing and breakeven-stop lessons.

style: retail FX swing/scalp, technical (fib, pivots, oscillators)
edge_principles: Focus on a single instrument until you know its 'personality', then add more.
End-of-day review ('scouting report') noting levels where price reacted and what must happen next day to continue or reverse.
Calendar all scheduled macro releases for the month in advance and plan around them.
Scaling into losers without a hard stop led to a margin call; use hard stops when away from screens and never trade on vacation from a phone/tablet.
Chasing price after alerts fire is a recurring leak.
notes: First-year retail FX trader; one loosely specified fib-confluence setup, mostly lessons about stops and preparation.

style: prop equities day trader (reversals), Kershner Trading Group
edge_principles: In a regime change, stop applying calm-market timing: panic lows arrive later/deeper, so wait for a bigger washout before buying reversals.
In high-opportunity regimes it is acceptable to take more calculated risk because recovery opportunities are abundant; in dead markets tighten risk.
Size up only when month-to-date profits give a cushion.
Manage the P&L window sorted from losers to winners: actively cut losers, leave resting exit orders on winners.
Do not anchor on 'it cannot fall further'; cut and re-enter later if the setup re-forms.
Short-sale-restriction (uptick rule after a 10% drop) changes how shorts and squeezes behave.
notes: March 2020 crisis-trading interview; reversal tactics adjusted for crash volatility, plus a capitulation-day bottom heuristic.

edge_principles: Do not bet against an unlimited central-bank backstop; the issuer of the currency cannot run out of money.
Credit spreads (IG and high yield) and on/off-the-run spreads are the stress gauges that drive central-bank action, more than equities.
notes: Explainer on Fed QE mechanics during March 2020; macro context only, no intraday setups.

style: prop market maker in oil derivatives (Onyx Commodities)
edge_principles: When everyone is already positioned one way, very bearish news that fails to move price lower is a sign of saturation; watch the reaction to news more than the news.
Express a view in the instrument that actually reflects it (differentials/time spreads track physical reality better than the headline future).
Market makers carry residual hedged (spread/box) risk overnight, positioned for the next time zone's flow; keep outright delta near zero.
Weekend news gaps leave no chance to exit; know your weekend exposure.
notes: Oil market structure during the 2020 price war; no intraday stock setups. The 'bad news, no follow-through' idea is a general sentiment tell.

style: journalist (book on Navinder Sarao and the 2010 flash crash)
edge_principles: Sarao reportedly made most of his career profit on a small number of extreme down days; a scalper's P&L can be dominated by high-volatility sessions, so be fully engaged and sized up on those days.
Patience: watching the ladder for hours and only acting at chosen spots.
Order-book signals (large resting orders) can be fake; spoofing is illegal and not a strategy - do not rely on visible size.
notes: Story of the 'flash crash trader'; spoofing is illegal and not usable. No legitimate setups extracted.

edge_principles: Leveraged/inverse ETFs rebalance daily (or when exposure drifts out of band), so they track daily, not multi-day, index returns.
ETF price is anchored to NAV by market makers/creation-redemption; visible ETF order-book size is not informative in the way it is for stocks.
ETF fund flows (e.g. heavy buying of inverse funds) are a usable sentiment gauge.
Index rebalance trades are executed at the close on rebalance dates.
notes: ETF mechanics explainer; no setups. Possible MCF idea: inverse-ETF volume spikes as a contrarian sentiment feature.

style: prop equities day trader, SMB Capital (first full year)
markets: US stocks, high-beta names, index ETFs
edge_principles: Review stats by time of day; he lost consistently 12:00-14:00 and stopped trading then, concentrating on the first hour.
Cut everything outside your proven playbook; early losses came from feeler trades, unfamiliar symbols, thin names and repeating the same failed idea several times.
Risk a fixed fraction of the daily stop per setup type (e.g. a third for A setups, a quarter for others).
Size up mechanically: every ~10 net-green trading days, size and daily stop rise 25%.
Exit into extended, volatile candles: sell strength / cover weakness.
Use VWAP as the 'who is in control' line for in-play stocks.
A handful of outsized days a year make most of the P&L; be prepared and sized for them.
notes: SMB first-year trader; concrete pre-market-range reclaim setup and VWAP-based trend/backside trades in parabolic names.

style: HFT infrastructure (shortwave links), ex-algo trader, Bookmap origins
edge_principles: Latency-sensitive opportunities are winner-take-all; a retail/bar-based system cannot compete on speed and should avoid edges that decay in milliseconds.
Lead-lag between correlated instruments (ES leading DAX, index futures leading stocks) is the main signal HFTs pay to see first; at bar resolution such lead-lag is already arbitraged.
notes: Infrastructure/latency episode; no setups usable at MCF's 5-min resolution.

edge_principles: Short-horizon signal half-life can be 1-3 months; monitor live edge continuously and retire decayed signals without attachment.
Use a selection layer that turns signals on/off by regime rather than running everything always.
Target only a small share (about 1-3%) of a product's average daily volume to stay within capacity.
Calendar/event metadata (holidays, Fed meetings, filings) must be wired into automated strategies.
Do not overpay for marginal speed; look for lower-hanging fruit in better signals or longer holding periods.
A backtest shown once with full disclosure of methodology is more credible than a cherry-picked best run.
notes: HFT fund-building story; principles on signal decay and capacity, no setups.

guest: Compilation (Anand Sanghvi, Jared Tendler, Michael Samuels, John Moulton, Mike Bellafiore, Nishant Porbanderwalla, Jack Ma, Tom Sosnoff, Dan Shapiro)
edge_principles: Asymmetric daily management (Dan Shapiro): a day that starts strongly is a 'premium hand' - do not stop at a fixed P&L goal; a day whose first trades fail within ~30 minutes should be cut off rather than pressed.
Hide the live P&L so exits follow the setup, not the dollar swing.
Never convert a short-term trade into a longer-term one because it is losing; mid-trade plan changes are usually bad.
Grade trades on process quality, not outcome; a winning trade that broke the plan is a bad trade.
Emotion accumulates across losing days ('tilt'); journal to discharge it and recognise revenge/desperation trading.
Many 'psychology' problems are really lack of edge (Bellafiore); verify the edge first.
Progress in small steps (lose less, trade flat, then small monthly targets); prop desks see substantial P&L only around year three.
Do not hold intraday positions into the close by accident; an unexecuted closing order once produced a huge overnight loss on news.
After a slump, step back and check whether the tape's behaviour has changed before re-engaging.
notes: Psychology compilation; one useful MCF-relevant rule is the day-level asymmetry (press good starts, stop after a poor start).

guest: Compilation (Lance Beggs, Ryan Trost, Tom Dante, Turney Duff, Tom Basso, James King, Charlie Bathgate, Peter Tao, Jared Tendler)
edge_principles: Think about who is trapped and whose exits will push price your way (the 'meta game').
Good trading means following your strategy that day, not making money (Tom Basso via Van Tharp); change systems only outside market hours.
Over-filtering a system to remove losers tends to remove the few large winners that pay for everything.
Know the base rates of your patterns; many publicly called setups have low strike rates.
Liquidity can change structurally (e.g. OTC routing) and turn a 1x planned loss into 3x; re-check fill quality when a niche changes.
Identify your 'C-game' recurring errors; repeated errors despite more market knowledge point to an emotional cause.
Sleep and health compound into performance; small 1-2% improvements add up over a career.
notes: Psychology compilation; only Lance Beggs' weak-pullback idea is a (loose) setup.

style: fund manager, quality-growth long equities with ETF hedging
edge_principles: About 90% of institutional orders (per his broker) are VWAP algos; they slow buying when price is above VWAP and save volume for the closing auction - VWAP is a real institutional reference.
Institutions often cap participation (~10% of volume) to avoid moving price; persistent same-direction flow over days in illiquid names signals a large unfilled order.
Repeated broker 'sell lines' in a held stock are a cue to investigate fundamentals.
Cut losers and hedge quickly; a fast index-ETF hedge added large relative returns in March 2020.
Monitor positions as weights and forward upside, not as red/green P&L, to reduce emotional decisions.
Wary of mean-reversion bets on valuation gaps: someone may know why the gap exists.
notes: Institutional process and execution-algo explainer; useful for understanding intraday VWAP-driven flow.

style: quant fund (Logica Capital), long volatility / mean expansion
edge_principles: Long-volatility (calls and puts) positions bleed in quiet markets; offset the bleed by trading around the core position - trimming into short-term extensions and re-adding on dips - while keeping the convex exposure.
Overfitting happens during testing too: if a hypothesis fails, do not nudge parameters until it passes; change a parameter only with an a-priori reason, otherwise abandon the idea.
Spend more time designing the experiment than running it; expect most ideas to fail.
Run the same idea at several holding frequencies (daily, bi-weekly, monthly) so one timeframe's 'wrong' call is hedged by another.
Published white-paper factors are crowded; prefer proprietary formulations.
Passive index inflows ('if cash then buy') structurally reinforce momentum and V-shaped recoveries; use macro structure, not forecasts, to set cadence.
Media/sentiment mostly reflects the last few days' price and has little forecasting value.
notes: Volatility-strategy and research-method episode; key research-hygiene lesson on parameter tweaking; no intraday setups.

style: prop firm founder, mathematical-edge trader, ex blackjack card counter
edge_principles: Small edges (0.25-1%) become meaningful only with leverage and hedging (pairs), which makes financing costs part of the edge.
Know how brokers, clearing firms and exchanges make money (borrow fees, order flow); fees can exceed the gross edge - he once made $2.5M and paid $3M.
Hedge everything: pair a short with a related long so only the edge is exposed.
Scale the exposure of a volatility-dependent edge up and down with realised volatility.
After several losing days, cut size only if you cannot identify what changed in the market; if the edge is intact, keep size.
Look for calendar niches (Mondays, month-end) where flows repeat.
notes: Veteran's view on math edges; one concrete, testable leveraged-ETF decay trade (borrow data is the gap).

style: retail small-cap short seller (ex e-sports pro)
edge_principles: Hard daily max loss set at the broker was the single fix that stopped account blow-ups.
Systematise entry and exit triggers so they can be back-tested from saved chart screenshots and executed without hesitation.
Normalise risk in R; compound R as a % of a notional account until a target R, then 'freeze' it for 1-3 months before stepping up.
Low win rate (~26%) is fine with ~6R average winners; use small starters cut at -0.5R and add only on confirmation.
Avoid fighting hot sector momentum even in 'garbage' stocks; sector waves (e.g. cannabis) caused his big drawdown.
Do not tighten the stop just to force a 3:1 ratio; get R:R by scaling into a working trade.
Withdraw surplus profits regularly and treat trading as a paycheck rather than a high score.
Allow a number of re-entry attempts proportional to expected reward, then stop.
notes: Clear small-cap backside short framework with R-based risk model and explicit stats.

style: prop equities (Seven Points Capital), discretionary momentum and small-cap shorts
edge_principles: Beginners should learn trend-joining pullbacks rather than reversal picks; better reward/risk and easier execution.
Squeeze warning signs for shorts: breakdowns that do not follow through, new highs after 10:30-11:00 in a low float, and volume far above the float without price falling.
Daily lockout = average green day over the last 21 days, so a max-loss day only gives back about one good day; unlock only if not on tilt.
On a losing streak halve daily risk, and halve again, until green days return; then size back up.
Write a per-setup list of allowed exit reasons and grade exits against it.
Need 30-40+ trades per setup before judging it; track stats by setup (separate accounts help).
New strategies go to a 'lab' at small size and graduate to more capital only when they work.
In quiet markets do less; do not use experiments as an excuse to be busy.
Only winning day trades may become overnight holds.
notes: Listener Q&A with a prop firm partner; several small-cap short patterns and strong risk-control rules.

markets: US-listed stocks incl. China reverse mergers
edge_principles: Red flags for fundamental shorts: margins far above peers, sudden last-minute rescues, executive history, heavy reliance on 'adjusted' metrics tied to management bonuses, debt-funded roll-ups that overpay.
Verify claims through customers, suppliers, ex-employees and physical observation rather than management.
Even a correct thesis can be squeezed by a promotional press release; size short positions so a 100% move is survivable and keep a 'squeal point'.
Build positions at no more than ~5-10% of daily volume to avoid alerting the market.
notes: Activist-short research process; fundamental/forensic, no intraday setups. Shows that sudden PR can double a heavily shorted fraud.

edge_principles: Alpha comes from identifiable inefficiencies or indifference of other participants (e.g. sloppy institutional execution, passive index funds); when the cause changes, the old model stops working.
A large share of US equity volume now trades at the close (market-on-close), which matters for intraday strategy design.
Any mean-reversion model must account for index rebalance flows to avoid fading forced buying/selling.
Narrow (sector/company-specific) models and alternative data trade more fitting risk for stronger priors; out-of-sample R^2 of ~0.03 is a success in markets.
Individual quants are better off licensing signals than starting a fund.
notes: Trends in quant investing; one concrete index-reconstitution idea, plus a useful flag to avoid fading index flows.
